summary:
I’m terribly sorry I haven’t sent you a copy of my speech, but I don’t have one. I’m waiting for Them to run off Xerox copies, as perhaps Mike Bailey mentioned when he was down visiting you. Anyhow, I think it was a good speech. The audience of engineers at UBC stamped their feet mightily, which, I’m told, is a good sign. They did not, however, drop water-filled balloons on me, which, I’m told, is also a good sign. I met many pretty girls (or as I for­ merly said, lotsa foxy chicks), and a good time was had by all (as I would have once said, we got it all together). Anyhow, I’m residing now in Vancouver, B.C. on what I hope is a permanent basis. As I know you know, this is a lovely city. The people are wonderful. 

But I miss my old friends. Especially—and she’s become a sort of transcen­ dent figure looming ever more largely in my mind—the one particular girl I had hoped to bring with me, Kathy. The final week before we left, Kathy freaked out— that is, got frightened; she has never been out of the Bay Area in her life—and she tore up her ticket and fled. At first I didn’t miss her so much, up here; there were so many people to meet and so much to see and do. But now as the days go by I seem to miss her more and more. I supposed she sums up everyone down there whom I’ve lost, evidently forever. I keep thinking about her and won­ dering if she’s okay. Actually, I’m sure she’s fine, and it’s me that’s screwed up. I can’t get her to phone me, even collect. I got one tiny pencil...
